resources.name: Web Animations API
resources.role: Native element.animate() with a seekable Animation.currentTime; no library needed
resources.summary: Browser API that animates DOM and SVG elements with keyframes, timing and a document timeline. Each Animation can be paused and its currentTime set, so frames are seekable from outside, and document.getAnimations() lists every running animation, CSS ones included. GSAP-like seeking with no dependency, but no labels, nesting or plugins.
use_when: Small DOM or SVG motion that must be seekable with zero dependencies
Pausing and seeking every CSS animation on a page via document.getAnimations()
Over CSS keyframes when frames are captured by setting currentTime
avoid_when: Multi-element choreography with labels and nesting: GSAP
Spring physics: Motion or React Spring
Canvas or WebGL content: drive it from t directly
Path morphs, text splitting, motion paths: GSAP plugins
notes: 2026-10-26: Seek-then-capture determinism was not tested; the MDN page fetched does not describe currentTime, which is assumed from the spec.

assessment.rationale: Standard-track and not experimental in Chrome since 75 per MDN browser-compat-data; seeking is a core feature. GSAP stays the richer timeline.

resources.name: Web Audio API
resources.role: Browser audio graph; OfflineAudioContext renders deterministic audio faster than real time
resources.summary: Node-graph audio API for oscillators, buffers, filters, gain automation and analysis. A live AudioContext plays in real time; an OfflineAudioContext renders the graph to an AudioBuffer as fast as possible, which suits VCR. Encode the buffer to WAV and mux with ffmpeg. For audio-reactive visuals compute per-frame features from the decoded buffer: AnalyserNode is real-time, and under OfflineAudioContext needs suspend(t) per frame. No beat or onset detection.
use_when: Rendering generated sound effects or beds offline into a WAV, no dependencies
Audio analysis (FFT) feeding visuals, computed from a decoded buffer
Over Tone.js when you only need a few oscillators, filters or gain ramps
avoid_when: Musical scheduling, instruments and effects: Tone.js
Mixing and fading existing files: ffmpeg
Live playback during capture: not deterministic
notes: 2026-10-26: Autoplay policy and headless audio output not checked; OfflineAudioContext avoids both in principle.

assessment.rationale: AudioContext and OfflineAudioContext supported since Chrome 35 per MDN browser-compat-data; stable and standard-track.

resources.name: WebCodecs
resources.role: Frame-exact browser video/audio encoders and decoders; pair with a muxer
resources.summary: Low-level API (VideoEncoder, VideoDecoder, AudioEncoder, ImageDecoder, VideoFrame) for encoding and decoding media without a container. Feed it VideoFrames made from a canvas with explicit timestamps and it returns encoded chunks; a muxer such as Mediabunny writes the file. Frame-exact, unlike MediaRecorder. Needs fully specified codec strings; H.264 availability varies by build.
use_when: Encoding canvas frames to VP9, AV1 or H.264 in-browser with exact timestamps
Decoding source video frames to seek without ffmpeg
Over MediaRecorder when output must not depend on wall-clock time
avoid_when: Finished MP4 with audio mux and filters: ffmpeg
Container reading and writing: Mediabunny or WebAV on top
Cross-engine needs: Firefox support only from v130, so check
notes: 2026-10-26: Codec support in headless Chromium (H.264, AAC) not verified; check isConfigSupported at runtime. MDN page states dedicated-worker availability but not secure-context status.

assessment.rationale: Standard-track, not experimental; Chrome 94 shipped VideoEncoder, VideoDecoder, AudioEncoder and ImageDecoder per MDN browser-compat-data.

resources.name: WebGL
resources.role: GPU 3D and shader API (WebGL 1 and 2) beneath Three.js, PixiJS and most canvas libraries
resources.summary: The browser's OpenGL ES binding, in WebGL 1 and 2, used directly or through Three.js, PixiJS, OGL, regl and twgl. Rendering is a function of uniforms such as time, so frames can be drawn in any order. Headless Chromium falls back to software GL when no GPU is present, which is slow but works. Read pixels or screenshot the canvas.
use_when: Custom fragment shaders or GPU particles driven by a time uniform
Under Three.js, PixiJS or OGL: the default backend that works everywhere
Over WebGPU when headless or broad Chromium support matters today
avoid_when: Heavy compute or modern GPU features: WebGPU, where supported
Plain 2D drawing: Canvas 2D
Raw API verbosity: use Three.js, OGL, regl or twgl instead
notes: 2026-10-26: Software GL fallback speed in headless Chromium comes from general knowledge; not measured.

assessment.rationale: WebGL 1 since Chrome 9, WebGL 2 since Chrome 56 per MDN browser-compat-data; standard-track, not experimental.

resources.name: WebGPU
resources.role: Modern GPU and compute API with WGSL; Chromium coverage varies by OS and needs checking
resources.summary: Successor to WebGL with explicit pipelines, compute shaders and WGSL, used directly or via Three.js WebGPURenderer or TypeGPU. Secure contexts only. Chrome 113 shipped it on ChromeOS, macOS and Windows; 144 added Linux on Intel Gen12+. Headless capture needs a working adapter, so check navigator.gpu.requestAdapter() and keep a WebGL fallback.
use_when: GPU compute or heavy particle and simulation work beyond what WebGL handles
Three.js WebGPURenderer and node materials on a machine with a GPU
Modern shader pipelines written in WGSL
avoid_when: Anything that must render on any machine: WebGL
Headless or CI renders without an adapter: WebGL on software GL
Simple 2D: Canvas 2D
notes: 2026-10-26: Headless Chromium adapter availability and required flags were not tested.

assessment.version_seen: W3C WebGPU (Candidate Recommendation); MDN: limited availability
assessment.rationale: Chrome 113 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows; 144 adds Linux (Intel Gen12+); Firefox 141, Safari 26 per MDN browser-compat-data. Not Baseline, so fallbacks are required.
